title: Replication and Sharding Production Design Review

questions.question: Which statement correctly separates replication from sharding?
options: Replication divides keys among owners, while sharding stores copies of each key
Replication copies an ownership range, while sharding divides keys into ownership ranges
Replication always scales writes, while sharding only improves durability
They are two names for the same database operation
questions.explanation: Replication stores copies of the same range. Sharding partitions different keys into ownership ranges. A sharded production database often replicates every shard.

questions.question: One tenant sends 45% of all writes and tenant_id maps that tenant to one shard. Why will adding read replicas not solve the write hotspot?
options: Replicas remove the tenant_id from every record
Replicas force every read to contact all shards
The copies still receive the same hot shard's write stream; they do not subdivide the tenant's ownership
A replication factor greater than one disables hashing
questions.explanation: Replication duplicates the hot ownership range. To divide that tenant's write load, the design needs a safely splittable key such as bounded buckets, plus the corresponding read and routing logic.

questions.question: Which shard-key property most directly reduces hotspot risk?
options: High cardinality with activity distributed across many stable values
A monotonically increasing value used as the leading range key
A mutable profile field that changes frequently
A low-cardinality status shared by most records
questions.explanation: High cardinality gives the system many placement units, and even activity prevents a few values from dominating. Cardinality alone is not enough if one value receives most traffic.

questions.question: A user updates a profile and must immediately see that write from a nearby replica. What is the safest routing approach?
options: Always use the replica with the lowest network latency
Wait a fixed second and assume replication completed
Read from a random replica and retry only on HTTP errors
Carry the write position and use a replica only after it reaches that position, otherwise wait briefly or fall back
questions.explanation: A session position turns read-your-write behavior into a verifiable routing condition. Wall-clock sleeps and process health do not prove that a particular mutation was applied.

questions.question: An asynchronously replicated remote region is 800 ms behind when the primary region is destroyed. What does that lag represent during promotion?
options: A guaranteed 800 ms read-latency increase only
A possible recovery-point window for acknowledged writes that had not reached the remote replica
A requirement to contact every shard for all future reads
Proof that the promoted replica contains every committed write
questions.explanation: With asynchronous replication, acknowledged writes can exist only in the failed region until replay reaches the remote copy. The measured lag bounds a potential, not automatically exact, data-loss window.

questions.question: Which sequence best describes a safe online shard move?
options: Delete source, update routers, then copy whatever remains
Let source and destination accept independent writes, then choose the larger copy
Copy a snapshot, replay changes, fence stale writers, atomically publish a new ownership epoch, verify, then clean up later
Change hash(key) mod N and wait for caches to expire
questions.explanation: Snapshot plus catch-up minimizes the cutover gap. Fencing and an atomic ownership epoch prevent two authorities, while delayed cleanup preserves rollback and verification options.

questions.question: Why can range partitioning by an increasing creation timestamp create a hotspot?
options: New inserts converge on the active tail range until it is split or moved
Range partitioning always sends each write to every shard
Timestamps prevent replicas from acknowledging writes
Ordered keys disable backup restore
questions.explanation: Although historical ranges may be balanced by bytes, current writes cluster at the newest boundary. The active range needs predictive splitting or a different distribution dimension.

questions.question: Why are replicated shards still backed up?
options: Backups make shard keys evenly distributed
Backups eliminate all cross-shard transactions
Backups prevent every primary failure
Deletes, corruption, and bad writes can propagate to every replica, so recovery needs an independent historical copy
questions.explanation: Replicas protect against copy failure, not every failure mode. A tested backup and log-replay path provide historical recovery after logical damage reaches all live copies.
